subtopic: REPORT OF SIR ALEXANDER GIBB TABLED
speechtext:
I desire to lay on the table of the house Sir Alexander Gibb's report on a survey of the national ports of Canada.
On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORT OF SIR ALEXANDER GIBB TABLED
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Marine if the report of Sir Alexander Gibb which has just been tabled will be printed and made available to every member of the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
subtopic: REPORT OF SIR ALEXANDER GIBB TABLED
speechtext: As members of the house can see, the report is voluminous. It contains many charts, plans and sketches, and to print it would be very, very expensive. I intend to refer the report to the committee on printing, and the committee will decide whe.her it should be printed in full or only a synopsis should be made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING:
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REPORT OF SIR ALEXANDER GIBB TABLED
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Marine, now that the report of Sir Alexander Gibb is down, whether it is the intention of the government at this session to introduce any legislation based upon the report?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
subtopic: REPORT OF SIR ALEXANDER GIBB TABLED
speechtext: The report is being studied now, and the question whether any legislation will be brought down will be under consideration within the next few days.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: VACANCY IN REPRESENTATION OF M AISON NEUVE
speechtext: I should like to draw the attention of the government to the fact that there has been a vacancy in the constituency of Maisonneuve ever since the sixteenth of January last. On the twenty-first of January the government issued a writ for a foy-election in Athabasca, where there was also a vacancy, but no writ was issued at the time with respect to the vacancy in Maisonneuve. I would like to ask if it was the intention of the government to allow that constituency to go unrepresented in this parliament this session; also whether the government intends to take steps to see that a writ is immediately issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: VACANCY IN REPRESENTATION OF M AISON NEUVE
speechtext: The Prime Minister is out of the house at the moment, but he will be in shortly and I will bring the matter to his attention and ask him to give an answer.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 10, to amend and consolidate the Fisheries Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Cowan (Port Arthur-Thunder Bay) in the chair.

Has this bill been reprinted, Mr. Chairman? I do not see how we can go on with it if it has not. It is not on our files. There was a large number of amendments, some of considerable importance, made to the bill in the marine and fisheries committee, and I do not see how we can intelligently study the bill unless it is reprinted with the amendments.

speakeroldname: The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Cowan, Port Arthur-Thunder Bay):
speechtext:
I understand that
the committee did not order the reprinting of the bill, that the amendments were short and that it was not considered necessary to reprint the bill.

I do not know what the
committee did not do, but it is not customary to discuss a bill with so many amendments in committee of the whole without first having the bill reprinted, and I have never heard that it was necessary for a committee to order reprinting;, that is a matter of departmental policy. I do not-see how we can adequately

deal with this bill. We trusted the amendments would be on record; we do not know what they are. For hon. members who have spent many days discussing this matter in committee it will be unfortunate if we have to begin all over again. I would suggest either that the amendments be printed in the votes and proceedings or that the bill be reprinted.

I wish to join in the
remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in requesting the minister to comply with the suggestion. I happen to come from a constituency in which great interest is taken in this bill. Not being a member of the fisheries committee I have no idea what amendments were made, and have not had an opportunity of attending discussions in committee. Therefore for the information of hon. members who have not attended the meetings of the fisheries committee I request that the amendments be printed or be put into such shape that they may be considered by the committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The amendments
adopted in committee were neither numerous nor very important, and for that reason the committee did not see fit to order reprinting. I wish to be courteous, however, and be as fair as possible to hon. members. If they think the bill should be reprinted, I have no objection. Therefore I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

The CHAIRMAN	(Mr. Cowan, Port

Fish Inspection Act

Will the minister introduce

Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes.

What section does that
amend?
Section 1 of the bill.

The confusion in this instance illustrates the need for the reprinting of the bill. We do not know what the amendments are. We have only a very imperfect recollection of what took place, and those hon. members who were not in the fisheries committee cannot possibly decide on the merits of the amendments.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these
clauses were embodied in the existing Fisheries Act. The suggestion was made in committee that this part of the Fisheries Act should be incorporated in the Fish Inspection Act because it concerns inspection. In the result therefore, we are deleting these clauses from the Fisheries Act and incorporating them in the Fish Inspection Act. There is no new legislation, but only a transfer from the Fisheries Act to the Fish Inspection Act. I do not think the amendments require printing.

Mr. Chairman, referring to
that part of the act which concerns oyster fisheries, I would like to call the minister's attention to regulations passed last year governing fishing for oysters. For instance, I find clause 12 is as follows:
"Minimum size of oysters." Except with the permission of the minister, no one shall fish for, retain or kill any round oyster of a less size than three and one-half inches in diameter, or any long oyster of a less size than four inches in length, of the outer shell.
In certain sections of the provinces of New Brunswick it will, be impossible to observe those regulations. The Caraquet bay oysters cannot be fished under that regulation at all. There is no use stating that if the regulations are observed the oyster will grow to a greater size. The natural shape of the Caraquet oyster is round. It is not elongated such as those found in Shediac bay or in Buctouche bay or Buctouche river. The result is that the men who have been able to earn their livelihood by the observation of former regulations are now thrown out of work. I ask the minister to look into these regulations very carefully, and to recommend that the sizes which obtained in the past be allowed. There is no use telling us that the regulations are enforced for the greater protection of the oyster beds. That may be true in certain sections of New Brunswick but certainly it does not apply to all sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I
thank the hon. member for the information and suggestions he is now making. He has referred to regulations, and I can assure him his suggestions will be well considered.

Since the minister has been so considerate in connection with my suggestion, I have a further one to make. In the name of conscience, do not allow oyster packages, as designated in the regulations adopted last year, to be used further. It is not a package that should be put on the market at all; it is too bulky and its appearance is enough to condemn the contents. Let us have a decent package. The inspectors of the minister's department have reported that the package is ungainly and unsightly, and I hope he will take that report into consideration. Some manufacturers of barrels submitted a certain plan, and that has been accepted. But simply because the plan meets their view is no reason why it should be accepted. The package most convenient to handle and best in appearance is the package that should be accepted, even if you have to put fewer oysters therein. If the package is to contain two, three or four hundred oysters, as the case may be, and this necessitates such an ungainly way of packing them, then reduce the number of oysters and put them in an attractive package. Do not impose on the public such an ungainly package as the one ordered last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am told that the fish dealers of Prince Edward Island are perfectly satisfied with the regulations as to those packages.
Fish Inspection Act
I may say to the minister that they are not satisfied. I am acquainted with hundreds of those dealers.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It will be a matter of investigation on the part of the officials of my department, and if my hon. friend's complaints are well founded no doubt we will take the necessary steps to remedy the situation.
What is the size of oysters under the old regulation and under the new?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not the information under my hand to-day, but I will supply it later on to my hon. friend.
Who asked for the change? Is it a departmental regulation or has it been requested by parties interested?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I cannot say offhand if it is purely departmental or if the change was made on the request of someone, but I wdll supply the information to my hon. friend.

In the past the regulation diameter was three inches for the round oyster and three and a half inches for the elongated; under the present regulations it is three and a half for the round and four for the elongated. There is no trouble about the four-inch diameter for the elongated oyster, but there is a great deal of complaint about the three and a half inch diameter for the round oyster. Whoever made the recommendation did not have in view the size of oysters in the different sections of New Brunswick and perhaps in Prince Edward Island. I can assure the minister that as to the Shemogue oyster, the Shediac oyster, the Buctouche bay and Buc-touche river oyster and the Baie du Vin oyster, there is no trouble applying the regulation, but when you come to oysters further north in New Brunswick you cannot apply it and do justice to the market, nor will the application of the regulation protect the oysters in northern New Brunswick.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 2-Containers must be inspected.

Section 2 was amended in the
twenty-third line, where the word "shall" has been changed to the word "need." The proviso will now read:
Provided that boxes for smoked herring and boxes for dry salted herring need not be inspected and marked until they have been packed and made ready for shipment.
Was there not another amendment made to that section?

All the words after the word "shipment" in line twenty-five were struck out. The amendment in so far as it relates to fish oil was also struck out.
Mr. NEILL; The same thing should be struck out in subsection 2.
It was.

When we pass this bill the
Angel Gabriel won't understand it. I find the member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) is driven to appealing to the house to do something for conscience sake.

Subsection 2 was amended by
striking out the proviso:
Provided that such fish oils as may hereafter come under the provisions of this act shall be prepared and graded in accordance with the regulations and be inspected in accordance therewith.

Carried.
Section as amended agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On section 4-Penalty for altering official mark.
No amendment to section 4?
No, but there was an addition to the old act.

Section agreed to.

Marine-salaries and contingencies, $437,137.

When will the deputy
minister be appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think it will not be long.
How long has the position been vacant?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

As the hon. member
for Quebec East knows, this is a matter for the Prime Minister, so I think the question should be directed to him when he is in the house.

Supply-M arine

I am hardly ready to
accept the doctrine that if the Prime Minister is not ready to appoint a deputy minister the department should not have one. Would my hon. friend subscribe to the principle, that even if he needs a deputy minister he will not have one if the Prime Minister is not ready to make the appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I did not say the
Prime Minister was not ready to make the appointment, but I have an assistant deputy minister and an assistant to the assistant, who are both very competent men. I do not think my hon. friend should press for an immediate appointment, because we want to make a first class choice.

Have any applications
been made to my hon. friend for the position?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

As I told my hon.
friend, any such applications must be made to the Prime Minister.

Not a word whispered

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

I wonder
if perhaps that is the reason why the appointment has not been made, all the applications going to the Prime Minister and none to the minister himself. I would not blame the minister if he did not make an appointment under those circumstances.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Ocean and river service-maintenance and repairs to Dominion steamers and icebreakers, $1,521,000.

I should like to direct
the attention of the minister, from my place in this house, to the situation with regard to the marine agency in the constituency which I represent. We have been somewhat unfortunate in the past in regard to the boats provided by the government. Many years ago, prior to the war, we had a good boat known as the Simcoe. Owing to the exigencies of the war that boat was taken from that station and sent to the Atlantic coast, for which work it was totally unsuited, as was shown by the fact that it was lost with all hands on its first voyage.
Subsequently a boat built for the St. Lawrence service, the C.G.S. Grenville, was placed on that route. This was a first class boat in every way, but it was rather small for the service. Two or three years ago the government purchased a vessel known as the
St. Helier, which I am led to believe was built during the war for coastal patrol work in Great Britain. This boat had an overall length of 130 feet. It was unsuited for the service and was unseaworthy in many ways, and a number of sister ships were lost. This boat was purchased by the late government on condition that it was to be lengthened to 180 feet, which was done, but no provision was made for changing the location of the engines. As a result when they attempted to turn her over to the captain and crew at Prescott she was found to be 14 feet down by the stern. In order to remedy that I understand about 200 tons of cement were placed in her forehold. In many ways she is absolutely unseaworthy, or so I am informed; she is cranky, and naturally must be under the conditions I have named. Any man with any marine experience at all will understand that the steering apparatus, the rudder and so on, built for a boat 130 feet in length, would be totally unsuited for a boat 180 feet long.
I would ask the minister to have this boat inspected by a thoroughly competent naval architect before it is placed in the service. The members of the crew, together with their families, are naturally apprehensive as to their safety. I neglected to mention that we had another boat in that service called the Lamb-ton, which also belonged to the Department of Marine and which was lost in lake Superior with all hands simply because it was not suited to the work. I think I am quite justified in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister, because I believe the government would be negligent if they did not look fully into it before risking the lives of the crew of this boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I had no knowledge
of the facts just brought forward by the hon. member; I always thought, and it was the opinion of the department, that the vessel in question was quite seaworthy. But I will be pleased to have an immediate inspection made by a competent officer. I am anxious to give the best service possible in that direction, and this will be done immediately.
I did not intend to reflect on the minister at all; this boat only came to the station late last fall, and we had no previous experience with her.

While this item is only for
maintenance and repairs it might be a proper time to ask the minister if he has carried out what I believe was his intention, the construction of a sister ship to the Estevan to aid in the lighthouse work on the Pacific coast. I presume the minister knows this vessel is
Supply-Marine

very badly needed. The Estevan is continually at work and the work has increased very much in late years, in fact, to a really marked degree, along with the development of the country. In years gone by they used to have three steamers, whereas now they have practically only one, the Estevan, with any equipment to lift the big buoys. For the lack of a sister ship or some auxiliary boat, we find that this powerful boat is going around doing what I would call petty work, such as a smaller boat would be suited for. Driven by necessity, therefore, they have allowed the lifting of buoys to get behind, so that the light goes out, and to try to meet the immediate situation they have adopted a sort of temporary system which takes up a good deal of time and is by no means satisfactory. All this is due to the fact that the vote is not sufficient to take care of the work. It was the intention of the department some years ago to build a steamer. Possibly this is being done now; the boat may be under construction. I cannot too strongly emphasize, however, the importance of another steamer on that work on the Pacific. I have not the figures with me, but if I remember rightly, in the last ten years the lights and buoys on the Pacific coast have increased one hundred per cent although the equipment to handle the work has gone down, from the standpoint of numbers at any rate. Can the minister give me any information in regard to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Though the department is fully seized of the necessity for such construction, we did not consider the time opportune to incur the expenditure, especially in view of the reduction in our revenues. We have decided not to undertake such expenditures at the present time, but we have the matter in hand and hope to be able, as soon as possible, to proceed with construction.

Is it the intention of the minister to go on with the project which the department contemplated two years ago, of building a new boat to replace the Jalobert, at Rimouski? I understood that plans were being prepared and estimates were obtained, and that it was proposed to go on with the construction at the earliest possible date. As the minister knows, the Jalobert is a small boat and the conditions under which she is operating at Father Point are extremely dangerous at times. The construction of a new boat is absolutely needed.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
That very question
was brought to the attention of the department two or three years ago and has been under consideration since. I regret, however, that I must give to my hon. friend the same answer I gave in the other case: the time is not opportune to undertake such expenditures. Unless it becomes absolutely necessary, I do not think we should go on with that undertaking at the present time.

If the minister will take the trouble to peruse the reports on file in regard to the Jalobert, he will see that it is becoming increasingly necessary every year to provide a new boat, and I hope he will give due consideration to the application already made.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I can promise the hon. gentleman that I will personally look over the last report and inquire into the matter.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
To provide subsidies for wrecking plants- Quebec and British Columbia, $40,000.

I notice that this vote has
been reduced almost fifty per cent, and knowing the minister's desire to be fair I am quite sure that most of this cut has been taken off Quebec rather than from the Pacific ocean. I should like the details, and particularly information as to where the paring has been done-I mean, what services.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The cut was from the Quebec Salvage Company grant.
What amount has been deducted from that subsidy so far as Quebec is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The department was
under contract with the Quebec Salvage Company-
With the Canadian Pacific Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -and is still under contract until the first of May. It is the Quebec Salvage Company.
Canada Steamships.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Well, I know that the Canadian Pacific Railway is greatly interested, and I am not sure whether to-day it does not own the majority of the shares. I can say, however, that the majority of the shares are to-day in the hands of Canadians and Canadian firms. It was suggested last year, when my estimates came before the committee, that the majority of the shares of that company were American, but that is not the case today. The contract expires on May 1. With the Pacific Coast Salvage Company we have a ten year contract expiring in 1935, so that we have made no change in the subsidy.
That is the explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
As to the Quebec
Salvage Company, we had to cut down expenses here and accordingly we intimated to the company that we could not grant the same amount after May 1 next.
Do I understand that the subsidy will not be renewed after May 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It will be renewed in the sum of $30,000.
Has the minister received any applications from other wrecking companies for similar subsidies, and have those applications been refused?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I cannot say that applications for grants have been received, but we have received communications from the Maritime Foundation and Wrecking Company, which operates a plant at Rimouski. They have asked that a grant be not given to any other company in order that they may be able to compete. After due consideration we came to the conclusion that we should reduce the grant to the other company, but we. could not cut it out entirely.

The minister has received from the Maritime Foundation and Wrecking Company a statement to the effect that they are able to carry on all the wrecking work in the gulf of St. Lawrence right up to Rimouski without receiving any grant. Notwithstanding this fact, he is granting a subsidy to cover that part of the river lying between Quebec and Rimouski, which subsidy has been paid to the company for the past twelve or fifteen years.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We have had proof that this company is operating its plant at a loss and under the circumstances we thought it only fair to maintain the grant.

Will the minister give the Maritime Foundation and Wrecking Company of Rimouski the same consideration given to the Quebec and British Columbia wrecking companies? If a grant of $30,000 is to be paid to the other company, does the minister not think that this company should receive some consideration? This company paid for half the cost of construction of the wharf and necessary dredging work at Rimouski, something which no company has ever done before. If this grant is to be renewed on May 1, does the minister not think that in all fairness it should be divided between the two companies? I think this is a very moderate request to make and I hope the minister will give it due consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The Quebec Salvage Company has always given first class service.

So has the Foundation company.
Supply-Marine

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We have no assurance that that company always will maintain a plant for salvage purposes. We must all realize the importance of being assured that first class salvage service will always be available on the St. Lawrence. The Foundation company organized its plant at Rimouski one or two years ago; this was not done at the request of the department as we were perfectly satisfied with the service given by the Quebec Salvage Company. If another company opens up a plant, is it fair that the grant should be divided? Suppose a third company starts to operate on the St. Lawrence, would it be fair to divide the grant by three? Suppose a fourth company opened up, would it be fair to divide it by four? We must be assured that we will always have a first class salvage organization on the St. Lawrence, and that is why the grant has been made up to date and that is why we have come to the conclusion that we should maintain that grant to the extent of $30,000.

I do not think the minister is being exactly fair to the Foundation company. He should remember that two years ago when the Department of Public Works agreed to construct the wharf at Rimouski, this company was compelled to pay half the cost of that work. They paid their bills and they paid for the dredging at Rimouski. They were assured that they would be given fair and due consideration and they have simply made a protest to the department that as far "as their company was concerned it was unfair to give a substantial subsidy to a company that had received a subsidy for a great number of years. The Quebec company has hardly been operating as far as the lower St. Lawrence is concerned. The company at Rimouski is operating the most powerful tug on the lower St. Lawrence and their assistance has been called for by the Quebec Salvage Company. To all intents and purposes the Foundation company is doing all the work down there, and the arguments advanced by the minister hardly apply as far as the Maritime Foundation and Wrecking Company is concerned or as far as the city of Rimouski is concerned. I refer particularly to the distribution of coal for the Canadian National Railways in the section between Moncton and Levis, and also to the distribution of the fertilizers which have been accumulating at Rimouski for the last few years. In view of the service which the Foundation company has given, in view of the assistance given in the construction of the
[Sir Eugene Fiset.l
wharf and the reduction of our unemployed,
I ask the minister to give further consideration to this matter. I ask him not to continue to give the reasons he has given for refusing this request. When this contract is to be renewed I ask him to take all these facts into consideration and divide the grant which he proposes to give to the. other company.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not want my hon. friend to understand me as criticizing the operations of the Foundation company; that company is a very reliable one and is doing a large business in Canada. As a matter of fact, it carried out undertakings at St. John, New Brunswick, both for the department and for the harbour commission; it took a large part in the work of reconstruction after the fire which occurred last year. The department is on the best of terms with this company but I do not think it would be fair at the present time to divide the grant between the two companies. This company has been operating only for a year or two and I think it should be allowed to continue for another year or two before we either wipe out all grants or decide to divide them between the two companies.
It may be quite true that this company has been operating at Rimouski only for a couple of years, but it had been operating in other parts of the lower St. Lawrence for many years before that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In Newfoundland.

The minister will admit that as far as emergency calls are concerned, the fact that this company is located at the entrance to the gulf enables them to render a better service than a company operating out of Quebec. I ask the minister to give this company an equal chance, or at least cut out all subsidies. I realize that he has given this company extremely fair consideration in the past, but I am talking for the city of Rimouski. I am going to try to get everything possible for Rimouski, notwithstanding what the minister may say.

Do I understand correctly
that this contract will expire on May 1, at which time a new contract will be entered into?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes.

In these days when we are
trying to economize in every way, would it not be a good idea to call for tenders for this work? That is done in the Trade and

Supply-M arine
Commerce department where they are subsidizing different steamship companies. I would suggest to the minister that instead of handing over this contract again to the Quebec Salvage Company he call for tenders and see which company is willing to do the work the cheapest. As the minister said a moment ago, this new salvage company may not stay in the business for very many years and therefore in calling for tenders he need have no fear that the department would not be properly protected. I would suggest that he call for tenders for a contract period of ten years and let the firms on the St. Lawrence tender for this work.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine

I am afraid that this is an example of that economy which is expensive in the long run. It is all . very well to economize where the economy involves at most only inconvenience. For instance, nowadays we sometimes ring up a $4,000 man in a department and a $2,400 man takes several minutes time getting the $4,000 man. Then the $4,000 man leaves his office unattended and walks along a corridor to the phone and communicates with the person who is calling him, and perhaps that process is repeated again a couple of minutes later-this in order to save a, phone. I do not think that is true economy, but at most it involves only inconvenience and delay. But to exercise economy in a vote of this kind strikes at the very root of the matter. It is economizing at the possible expense of human lives. I know that west coast like a book, and these life boats are not fit to be taken out in winter with only a skeleton crew. The minister mentioned six men: but one must always be left at home as a watchman, and so forth. It has been found from experience that to man these boats adequately, and they are pretty big boats, so that they can put out to sea and reach the scene of a wreck, you must maintain more than six men in the winter time. I deprecate very much the suggestion of economizing in that way. I have not raised my voice in the house this session to protest against any other economy, painful and awkward as it has been in connection with many of the estimates. I am of opinion that such a change would imperil the lives of the crew and the usefulness of their operations. Of those six men one must constantly attend to the engine, another must steer, and another be in charge of the remaining three. Those four men would have to do the work of taking the people from a wreck while perhaps holding the boat off rocks, and so forth. If the minister has made his decision I can do no more than enter my protest.
At this time I should like to mention another point, which I had intended to raise during the discussion on the bill to reduce by ten per cent the salaries of civil servants. These wretchedly paid men receive only $65 per month. They are not stenographers here in Ottawa receiving only $65 per month, but they are men who maintain families and if called upon have to go out and risk their lives. In fact they must do that, or they would be of no use; and for those services they receive only $65 per month. In addition they receive $25 for board allowance making their total remuneration $90 per month. The $25 allowance how-

ever is not as beneficial to them as it would be to some one working in Ottawa, because those men are married and must maintain their homes, and the $25 just pays for their food on board ship. Therefore they are receiving considerably less remuneration than some workmen on shore. Of the $90 per month only $65 is available, because the $25 has to go to their mess.
Under the bill now going through this house stipulating a cut of ten per cent, these men receiving $1,080 per year will be cut $108, because they are not eligible for superannuation. They would like to have that benefit, but through the operation of some legal quirk they are not allowed to qualify. A case has been decided to that effect. If they were paying into a superannuation fund, by the provisions of the bill now going through the house the government would pay their superannuation allowances and they would be receiving a cut on their salaries of only five per cent, or $54. However, because they are not eligible for superannuation-because if they were to drown to-morrow their widows and children would receive no payment from the superannuation fund-they are to be taxed, forsooth, ten per cent. The cut is levied on the full salary of $1,080, whereas in my view it should be only five per cent and based on the monthly salary of $65, or the yearly salary of $780. Surely in such cases special consideration should be given. They are receiving less than $1,200 per year, and whether or not they are paying into a superannuation fund, they should not be docked more than five per cent.
As the bill reads to-day-and undoubtedly it will pass in its present form-these men receiving the miserable salary of $65 per month, or at the very most $90 per month, are going to be docked ten per cent simply because through an interpretation of the law they are not eligible for superannuation. Can we expect those men to be enthusiastic about their work when they see men receiving salaries greater than theirs docked only five per cent, and when they realize that from the beggarly renumeration I have mentioned will be cut ten per cent. I hope the minister will take steps to consider this injustice, and at least make an effort to arrange that these men be deducted only five per cent, the same as they would have been had they been paying into a superannuation fund. That is as good an illustration as I can think of; these men who are poorly paid and receiving only $1,080 must submit to a ten per cent cut, whereas other men receiving superannuation benefits are docked only five per cent. The fact is that they are really receiving only $780, and

I am quite sure the minister will realize the justice of my suggestions and that he will do all within his power to get- I am not asking at present for better remuneration, although they certainly ought to have it-special consideration of their case whereby the cut may be reduced from ten per cent to five per cent.

I understand that this ship is intended to ply in Pacific waters and tenders for its construction were called for and the lowest tender accepted. If there is only about $50,000 difference between the lowest and the next highest tender, I think it would be safe to say that the difference between wages paid in British Columbia shipyards and those paid in Collingwood would amount to more than $50,000. I am not strongly in favour of giving a contract to the lowest tenderer when it is manifest that the difference will be taken out of the labouring man. This practice is conducive to the payment of low wages, and is against the very basis of the fair wage policy of the federal government. Contractors should not be permitted to accept contracts on the cutthroat method, as we used to call it; they should not be allowed to make a low tender and then take it out of the pockets of the working man. I am quite satisfied that if the difference in wages paid on the Pacific coast had been taken into account, there would be

found to be a difference of more than $50,-000-perhaps even $100,000-in the total payroll. I think the minister should look into this matter to see that no contracts are awarded to contractors, manufacturers or construction concerns who pay the lowest wages.
Was a tender received from the Prince Rupert Dry Dock Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If my memory serves me aright, one was received but it was for a very high figure. I can give my hon. friend definite information in this regard if he so desires.

Was the fact that this company is owned and operated by the government taken into consideration? When future ships are to be built, especially the Pacific coast service, I think this dry dock should be considered as it is operating on the Pacific coast and is subsidized by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I shall be glad to bear that in mind.
Has the minister any information as to the wages paid to the various craftsmen employed by the Collingwood shipyard as compared with wages paid in British Columbia shipyards?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not that information before me. I may tell my hon. friend that the Collingwood shipyard has subscribed to the fair wage clause. The company has been in conference with the then Minister of Labour (Senator Robertson) as to the rates of wages to be paid for the construction of this ship. We have always understood that we were obliged to accept the lowest tender, and that was the one received from the Collingwood shipyard.

The prevailing rates of wages at Collingwood might be .25 per cent lower than the rates paid on the Pacific coast, and consequently the workmen in British Columbia shipyards might be denied employment if this fact was not taken into consideration. When a ship is to be built for Pacific waters the contract for its construction should not be given to a shipyard in other parts of the country where a lower rate of wages prevails.
Especially when the government has a plant of its own.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Supply-Marine-Radio
Mr. Chairman, before the next item is called, may I ask the minister if he will agree to having items numbers 148 and 149 considered together, as they both relate to radio service?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have no objection.

I think it would facilitate discussion.
Radio service, to provide for the construction and maintenance of radio ship to shore stations and the general administration of the provisions of the Radio Act and regulations throughout the Dominion, $716,000.
Radio service, to provide for the general improvement of reception conditions to licensed broadcast listeners, $180,400.

Mr. Chairman, there are
hundreds of thousands of radio fans in this country, and this year the cost of a radio licence has been increased from one to two dollars. These radio listeners are complaining about the fact that the service mentioned in item 149 is not what it should be. People purchase radios, some of them very expensive, and they are entitled to good service. The minister knows that the least trouble is a great handicap to radio reception, and that is why it was decided by the previous administration to organize a staff of part-time inspectors. Most of the present day radio sets are batteryless, they are connected to the lighting current and when trouble occurs in one machine, other machines on the same current feel the effects. These inspectors have special apparatus and they go throughout the community in an effort to eliminate trouble for the listeners. The licence fee has been increased, and of that we do not complain but on behalf of all radio listeners in Canada I would urge the minister to see that the number of radio inspectors is not reduced.
There is another matter-I have no personal interest in it beyond that of any other radio listener-and that is that those who will be working under this vote should be men well qualified for the work. In my home town the chief electrician of the city is doing this inspection work and doing it very well. He is provided with certain apparatus to help him locate troubles, and he is doing very well in eliminating trouble and improving reception conditions. I would ask the minister if it is his intention to retain the men who are now performing this work efficiently to the great benefit of all radio fans in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The hon. member's remarks are quite in order. The licence fee has been increased from one dollar to two
dollars. I agree with my hon. friend that the owners of radio sets who are paying a licence fee are entitled to first-class service, and my department will attempt to give the best service possible. When the estimates were brought before the house, I think, although I am not quite sure, that the licence fee had not been increased. I cannot make any definite promise to the committee, but if within a few days I come to the conclusion that the amount I am now asking the committee to vote is not sufficient to give a first-class service, I shall see that a certain amount is inserted in the supplementary estimates.

It will have to be
approved by the Prime Minister.

I thank the minister for his kind remarks. I would point out that the number of those inspectors is small, there being only one I believe in each town, and if the number of inspectors is reduced, some of the towns in this country, which ones we do not know, will suffer. I have been told that the dispensing with the services of thirty-seven of these inspectors is under consideration. The Canadian people do not complain so much of paying a licence fee of two dollars instead of one dollar, but I do submit that they are entitled to receive just as good service when they are paying a two dollar fee as when they were paying one dollar. If there is not a good inspection service, interference may be continuous, with no one to stop it, and the least little trouble may sometimes cause the reception to be such that a radio is not worth listening to. I urge the minister therefore to reconsider this matter seriously. If at the time his estimate was prepared it had not been decided to increase the licence fee, I would suggest that now that the fee has been increased, conditions are different and the decision with respect to this inspection service should be different, in the interests of the radio listeners of this country.

I have been asked by
a number of radio users in my province to say something of the same nature as has just been said. Throughout parts at least of the province of Alberta, and particularly in the smaller towns and villages, where the use of radio has become very extensive, people have urged, and have asked me to place the matter before the minister, that their complaints as to interference are not receiving the attention they should. They had no objection to paying a licence fee, even a higher fee than had been charged, provided that they got the
1844'
Supply-M mine-Radio

service, but they do feel, particularly the people in the smaller towns and villages, that the interference is too frequent and often from a cause which a qualified inspector would find trivial and could easily remove. Possibly there is not a sufficient number of inspectors; at all events adequate service was not given. They felt that they were not getting their money's worth. On behalf of these users of the radio I transmit this complaint to the minister, and now particularly as it has turned out that their anticipations of a higher licence fee were correct I would urge the minister, to see that the service is improved. As I have said, the people particularly in the small towns and villages feel that they are not getting the service to which they are entitled, that their complaints are left unremedied, and interference is allowed to continue.
While I am on my feet there is another matter I wish to mention. We all know that some aspects of the radio question are now before a committee of this house, and I would ask the minister if it is not possible that from the report of that committee recommendations may come and changes be made which would completely alter the whole aspect of things so far as the present estimates are concerned. Or is it more likely that any such changes will be for the future and will not affect the estimates of this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I do not think that
the findings of the committee will affect in any way the estimates of this year. I quite agree with what the hon. gentleman has said with regard to interference troubles in the province of Alberta, and that the service should be improved, and it is the intention of the department to appoint a greater number of inspectors in that province.
I am very glad to hear the minister say so, because the use of radio is increasing very rapidly in Alberta.

We have one inspector for the city of Sydney, and I am in receipt of a letter from him to-day saying that his services are being dispensed with; consequently we will have no inspector in Sydney. I am anxious to know just what inspection service is being provided in a case like that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I understand that the services of the part-time inspector in Sydney have not been dispensed with. He is still in the service and we are considering the matter. Whether in such cases we will provide the service by using a local man or by using regular men in adjacent towns and cities is

under consideration. If we receive a larger amount for that service we will undoubtedly retain the services of the man to whom reference has been made, because I am told he is very efficient.

I
understand he has received notice that his services will not be required after the end of the month.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
He is still working
for the department.
I trust the minister will continue his services, because I understand he is well qualified.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I think we will be
able to satisfy the hon. member.

Can the minister estimate
the amount of money which will be received under the new rate of licence fee?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I can tell the hon.
member that at the rate of one dollar per licence we received last year the sum of $510,000 net, commissions having been paid. At the two dollar rate we expect to collect about $1,200,000.

Then, so far as that
part of the branch is concerned, we may conclude it is self-supporting?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, there is no doubt about that.

Although there is a reduction of $44,600 in the estimate, the minister tells us the figure was struck before the government decided to increase the licence fee. Would he give us the assurance that since the licence fee has been increased his department will see that more attention is paid complaints regarding interference?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that if we get the money we will give better service.

The department will be
receiving another $500,000.

When will the new
rate of two dollars come into force?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: On April 1.

Will the minister
see that proper advertising is given in the local press, not only in the county of Rimouski but throughout the district of the lower St. Lawrence river? In the constituency of Rimouski we have a newspaper called Le Progres du Golife, and advertisement could be made in that paper. When the rate of one

Supply-M arine-Radio
dollar was put into effect the people in the lower St. Lawrence district did not know to whom they were to pay the licence fees. There were no advertisements in the local press, and no posters in local post offices. Postmen were supposed to collect the fee, but unfortunately they told the people that they had no authority to collect. As a result an inspector came down to the town of Rimouski and prosecuted fifteen or twenty people who had not paid their licence fee because they did not know where to pay them. Now that a new rate is coming into force, I suggest that the minister advertise in the local paper, Le Progres du Golfe, and that posters be placed in post offices throughout the lower St. Lawrence district. I beg that this be done in the interests of the people of that district, and I am sure the department will benefit if they avail themselves of my suggestion.
At this time I should like to direct my remarks to another point. Two years ago the Department of Marine spent a great deal of money on new instrumentation of the Marconi station at Father Point. The new instrumentation was supposed to do away with static in the lower St. Lawrence region. The fact is however that conditions are worse than ever. If proper inspection of the new installations had been made by the department some of the difficulty might have been eliminated. I would ask the minister to issue instructions that inspection be made of the new installations to see if the condition can be remedied. The static is a nuisance to the radio fans in the county of Rimouski, and especially in the town of Rimouski. I assure him the whole population in our section of the country would be extremely obliged if he would have an inspection made with a view to improving conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have no objection to recommending a further inspection. I am told however by the chief of my department that the trouble does not arise from the station, but is due to the fact that during the summer months static is caused by the foreign boats going up and down the St. Lawrence river. I am happy, however, to accept my hon. friend's suggestion, and will have the station thoroughly inspected once more.

Will the minister
take the necessary steps to advertise as I have suggested?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes, although I do not promise that we will accept the particular advertising mediums suggested by my hon. friend.
The newspaper I mentioned is friendly to my hon. friends opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We will take steps to inform the people in the St. Lawrence district, and in every other part of Canada, as to the amount of the licence fee and where it should be paid.
I should like to ask the minister this question: From what point is the county of Huron served, and from what centre does the trouble man come?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I understand the man who attends to the trouble in the county. of Huron comes from Kitchener or London.

I quite agree with the
hon. member for Brantford City that since we are to derive such a large revenue we should get down to a system of county inspection. The cities of London, and Kitchener, Ontario, are from seventy to one hundred miles from some parts of my constituency, and I do not know that I have ever seen one of the trouble men who, the minister has told us, are located in London or Kitchener. I am told that the wagon passes through occasionally on fine days or holidays. We do not know who he is, we do not know where to send for him. I understood the minister to say that the radio licence was raised from one to two dollars to enable him to spend more to ensure radio listeners getting better reception. I contend that that was not at all necessary. During the first ten months of the past fiscal year the revenue of the radio department was 8494,648.26 and the expenditure $167,053.65. So the department was able to donate to the exchequer a third of a million dollars. In the preceding year, 1930-31, the net revenue was
Supply-M arine-Radio

$459,469.32, and the expenditure $221,655.90. I register my protest against the raising of the radio licence fee to two dollars, and I do so in a very orthodox fashion, because the minister will remember that as representing a county which I do not expect to have blotted off the map in favour of any other county, I asked him before any changes were made in radio policy to give me an opportunity of expressing my people's views in the matter. I believe that in my county of North Huron, regardless of politics, any person who has a radio, or expects to get one, objects to this increase in the licence fee, especially when the department had a surplus of a third of a million dollars for the first ten months of the past fiscal year. But not only is the increase in the licence fee objected to; this is only a start and we do not know where the minister or succeeding ministers may stop. In Ontario the government first imposed a war tax of one cent a gallon on gasoline, but they were not content with that and increased the tax to two cents, then to three, four, five and finally to six cents, and to-day they are actually apologizing that the tax is a cent lower than in some of the other provinces. As governments in the future look around for revenue I am just a little fearful, Mr. Minister, that the radio licence will be an awfully convenient place just to put on another dollar, and another year another dollar. I feel that my people have not been properly treated, inasmuch as their representative asked over a year ago that before any changes were made he should at least be given an opportunity to express their views to the minister. I do not propose to have the whitewash brush put over my constituency and any other constituency in the province painted red. I protest against this raise in the licence fee. It was not necessary to get more revenue to improve radio reception, for already you have far more revenue than you need. These are strenuous times, and if the department really wanted more money there might not be any very strong objection to an increase, but on the face of it there is no necessity for this increase and in any event we want to know exactly what the minister proposes to do with the additional revenue. While the radio committee is taking evidence I hope the minister is not a mile or two ahead of them and formulating a policy for which this increased revenue will be needed. Before anything of the kind is done, I for one wish to have an opportunity of presenting my views upon the matter.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. gentleman rightly under-

stood my remarks. I did not say that we increased the licence fee to $2 because we needed money to give better service to radio listeners. After studying the question very carefully the government came to the conclusion to charge radio owners a licence fee of two dollars. Maybe it is to help the exchequer, but if so, I am sure the radio listeners in North Huron as well as those in other constituencies will gladly contribute.
Is it to help the exchequer?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I am confident that radio owners will gladly help the country in this difficult financial situation. The government thought that 'any citizen who owns a radio and receives good service and hears all kinds of interesting programs would not object to paying a two dollars licence fee. Of course, the additional revenue will be a great help to this country, and I think when he has considered the matter carefully my hon. friend will share the views of the government on this question.

Then it is a tax, because the minister does not need this increased revenue for the purpose of giving service to radio listeners; he has more than sufficient money for this purpose under the one dollar licence fee. This increase is a tax. Why not say so?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: "A rose by any other name-".
Yes.

What proportion does the
number of licence fees collected bear to the number of radio owners?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I cannot tell exactly, but this year we have collected over $600,000 in radio licence fees. We intend to see that every radio owner pays the licence.
I think it would be far better for the minister to see that the licence fee was collected from every radio owner rather than increase the fee to $2 to the willing payer.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We hope every radio owner will be willing to pay this licence fee. If we come to the conclusion that all those owning radios have not taken out their licence we will have our inspectors take the necessary steps to enforce payment.

On that point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister that the present system of collecting the licence fee is not very satisfactory. It is left to the option of the individual radio

Supply-M arin e-Radio
owner to go to some person in the locality who has the sale of radio licences. But the honest man is up against this difficulty. The local licence distributor in the past was required to buy the licences in books of ten, valued at one dollar apiece, for which he sent $9 to some central office. He might have several of these books on hand for months without disposing of the licences, with his money tied up in the meantime, and this made him very reluctant to buy sufficient books in advance to meet the local demand. I know that radio owners in my constituency have found it very difficult to get a licence when they wanted it. The local distributor would not have any licences on hand, and weeks later those desiring licences would find him still without a supply. He put up the argument that it was not fair that he should be required to invest his own money in those books without knowing how many individual licences would be required. Now with a two dollar licence it is going to be even worse. I was wondering if this point had been brought to the attention of the minister, and if there is not some better way of administration so that the licences will be there when the individuals come for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Since the increase to two dollars the question of collection has been under consideration. It may be that the system in force up to this time has not been as effective as it might have been, but we are studying the matter. We will see that everyone pays for his licence this year, and if we have to change our method of collection we will do so. The matter is under consideration.

I should like to ask the minister just what machinery there is for collecting these licences at present. In Saskatchewan, where the police are partly federal and partly, provincial, the mounted police undertake that responsibility, but what is being done in the other provinces where the federal government has nothing in the way of a police force? Surely there must be some machinery for checking up on these licences.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Licences are issued by the radio dealers, the banks, the post office branches and by any vendor who applies to the department for books of licences, as was mentioned by an hon. member a moment ago. Of the amount of $571,000 collected last year the radio dealers collected $416,069; the post office department $123,000 and the vendors $32,000. The radio dealers receive a commission of ten per cent; the post office staffs
get a commission of five per cent, and ten per cent is paid the other vendors. This year we intend to allow a commission of 15 cents on each licence, which is at the rate of 7i per cent.
As I told another hon. member, we are studying the question to-day in connection with the collection of these licence fees. It is a very important matter, and it is only fair that everyone who owns a radio should pay the licence. I hope to be in a position this year to collect the licence for every radio in Canada.

It appears that at present the government provides only the machinery for furnishing licences, and that there is no machinery for really enforcing the law, except in the provinces where the mounted police operate. They are federal as well as provincial officers, but in provinces where there is only a provincial police force I take it that no one has any particular interest in enforcing the law. It means that if a citizen is law-abiding and takes out his licence everything is all right, but apparently there is no machinery for coping with the people who use radios but fail to take out a licence at all. That is the point to which I was referring.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, for the last two years the federal jurisdiction has been challenged by several provinces, including Ontario and Quebec, and during that period no prosecutions have been carried on. Since the question of jurisdiction has been definitely settled by the privy council, however, we intend to see that everyone pays his licence fee, and those who refuse to pay will be prosecuted in due course. Of course every opportunity will be given every citizen of Canada to pay his fee; if necessary, when a citizen is willing to pay we will give him ample time, but we intend to see that every citizen pays his licence fee.

If there were one hundred thousand radio owners in this country a fee of one dollar would bring in a total of $100,000. If the cost of administration of the department was $200,000 then I would agree that the licence should be increased from one to two dollars in order to give better service to owners of radios. On the other hand, however, if with $100,000 this department can be managed very well, I do not see why this increase should be made. The old Romans used to ask for bread and games, and human nature has not changed very much. Perhaps good radio service has done more than chapter 58 of 1931, for the peace, order and good government of this country.
Supply-Marine-Radio

I say that in lighter vein, but I am very serious about it. There are many poor people in the country who have very little to eat, who live in homes which are far from comfortable and who are consoled, while waiting for better times, by listening to concerts and speeches by my good friend the Minister of Marine and his leader, which come over the radio. These people are cheered, while waiting for better times, by being able to listen to the radio; when they feel depressed or distressed, to use a famous word, they turn the switch and hear a nice concert coming from Toronto, Montreal, New York or somewhere else. It gives them courage and helps them forget their trouble. This is a psychological fact, as everyone will admit-, so I say it is very important to make things easy for the poor people in order to give them a chance to hear good music at little cost. So I say that if the increase is to improve the service I am in favour of it, while if it is to plug a hole somewhere else I am against it.
I have great regard for the Minister of Marine; I am sure he speaks in good faith when he says he will reconsider the matter of inspectors. I hope that if when he does so he makes a favourable decision and he will not replace the old, competent men with new, incompetent men. In conclusion may I ask if there is to be any decrease in the number of men operating the radio beacons in the St. Lawrence river and in the gulf of St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I may tell the hon.
gentleman that there will be no decrease in the number of employees operating the radio beacons on the St. Lawrence, and I can also assure my hon. friend that competent inspectors who were employed last year will remain in our service during this year.

When this licence fee was first imposed it was generally understood by the public-and I believe the government made it clear at the time-that it was intended simply to provide service for radio owners. In the small towns and villages, throughout my part of the country at any rate, there is a great deal of trouble through interference from telephone wires, from small electric plants, and all that sort of thing. There are a great many difficulties in that way and it seems utterly impossible to get an inspector there to look into the situation. Inspectors, I know, are employed by the government, and when the radio owner pays his licence fee he expects to 
get in return just that kind of service. That was what the money was supposed to be for. In my part of the country we have found it impossible to get such service. I have personally complained to the inspectors at Regina and elsewhere, but I have not been able to get them to come to these little towns to investigate the trouble. In some small places, owing to imperfections in the lighting system, when the lighting plant is in operation it is impossible to hear anything. Will the minister assure us that in future we shall get, in return for the money we pay, some service that will enable us to use the radio under favourable conditions? Will he undertake to have these plants and telephone wires checked up so that the local authorities will know where the difficulty lies?

Following up the remarks
of the hon. member, I want to ask a question. When the inspectors discover such trouble as my hon. friend has mentioned, due to some power corporation or private plants, has the department the power to compel these people to remedy the condition that is causing the trouble, and are they doing so?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We have no power to order companies to stop their operations if they are causing trouble, but I am told that as a matter of fact when our inspectors locate any trouble the companies are always willing to see that a stop is put to it.
The trouble is chiefly with the small plants, and it would require little to remedy it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As a rule, the companies are quite accommodating. As to the service given in the province of Saskatchewan, we have to-day six regular men who go-around in cars the year round.
Six.men in the province of Saskatchewan alone?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes.
Then it is strange we do not see them in our part of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Perhaps there are no complaints from those parts.

There are complaints;
I can assure the minister that I have made many complaints myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I shall be pleased to look into the matter. I can assure the hon. gentleman that my department will give the best service possible in his part of the province.

Supply-M arine-R adio

I was very glad to hear the minister say that he would maintain an efficient radio inspection service. I received a letter this morning from the town of Fort Frances in northern Ontario, where the part time inspector has just received notice from the office of the department in Winnipeg to the effect that his services will not be required after April 15. There is no use repeating the arguments that have been made; suffice it to say that in that town and district we have a good deal of trouble. The town is about 250 miles from Winnipeg and about the same distance from the head of the lakes. I shall be glad if the minister will assure me either that a part time inspector will be kept on or that he will provide a full time inspector.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
When the notice was
given, the policy with regard to inspection had not been definitely settled, but we thought it advisable to give notice in order that we might be free to make any decision we thought fit. I can assure the hon. gentleman that Fort Frances will receive proper service. If it is necessary to keep on a part time inspector in that place, one will be maintained. At any rate, the matter will be inquired into to the satisfaction of the hon. gentleman.

The minister has
said tiiat since the privy council's decision his department will see that licence fees are collected without fail under the two dollar rate. I was wondering just what will be taken for granted with regard to the question whether a radio which has been installed is actually in use. I have been told that if a person has an aerial erected it is assumed that he is operating a radio. I would point out that at the present time in the west, in Saskatchewan at least, there are many aerials installed and perhaps many machines in the homes, although they are not in use owing to financial conditions. If that is the case, will the radio licence fee be required from such persons, irrespective of whether they use the machine or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If our inspector decides that the claim of the radio owner is bona fide, that he is not using the machine, no licence fee will be collected; but that claim must be bona fide. It happens sometimes that an owner in order to evade the law, disconnects his radio when he expects a visit from the inspector. As I say, his claim to have discontinued the use of the radio must be bona fide.
I hope the minister will broadcast that statement throughout Canada-that it is left to the inspector to decide whether the radio owner shall pay his licence fee or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I do not say it is
left to the inspector, because every owner of a radio is presumed to use his radio, and in that event he must pay the fee.

The minister said
that if the owner decided not to use the machine he had only to approach the inspector, and if reasons he gave were sufficient the licence fee would not be exacted. I ask the minister to publish that broadcast.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I say that if the inspector comes to the conclusion that the radio is not in use, I do not think he should charge the fee. I did not give that as a definite answer, because, as has been suggested, a man who does not use his radio should take it out of the house.

Where would he put
it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Our inspectors are
very fair; but, as I said, our intention is to see that every radio user shall pay the licence fee. It is only fair that everyone who is using a radio should pay.

Suppose a man who is in possession of a radio discusses with the inspector the fact that he is not using that radio, the decision should lie with the inspector who should be able to give a definite decision that in that case he shall not be compelled to pay the two dollars per year.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the inspectors are under the officials of the department.

Will they receive
instructions from the department to give a final decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:

The fee has been raised to two dollars and I understand that the revenue is to be used to employ inspectors to go round and see if people have paid their fee. A certain revenue would be received and it would not be necessary to have men going around the country in order to find out whether people are or are not using their radio sets.

I should like to leave a

These men could check up on licences, be advised of local troubles and then call in the experts, the mechanics and engineers whenever it was necessary. I remember I had to telegraph the predecessor of the present minister complaining of two men who had come into my town who did not act courteously in entering the homes of the residents. We have instances of men who come to a home and say they are gas inspectors but who eventually prove to be burglars, and it was because of this that I complained to the former minister. Upon investigation it was found that licences were not readily obtainable in our locality, and this matter was corrected. I should like to see appointed in my county some person who is known to the people and who could be conferred with. At the present time, practically all of these men seem to come from Kitchener: there might have been a good reason for that during the old regime, but that should not apply to the present regime.

On section 1-1921, c. 78, repealed.
Will the sponsor kindly explain the bill?

This bill is to repeal a special act of this parliament passed in 1921. The two inventions mentioned in the preamble had been in use for more than one year before the application for patent was filed, and therefore the patents could not be issued under the general act as it then stood. A special act was accordingly passed on June 4, 1921, empowering the commissioner to issue the two patents. In the same year the general act was amended and it changed the time limit during which applications had to be filed. This made the two inventions patentable under both the special act and the general act as amended, and the commissioner of patents in exercising his authority did so under the general act and not under the special act. Doubts have arisen whether the general act or the special act should be deemed to apply to the patents in question. In order to remove these doubts it is asked that the special act be repealed, and the patents will therefore be issued under the authority of the general act, under which, as a matter of fact, the (patents were actually granted by the commissioner.

What will be the
practical effect of the removal of the doubts?

If the general act had been as it is to-day, the special act would not have been required. Authority was given to the commissioner to issue the patents under both the special act and the general act as amended, both acts being assented to on the same day. It seems to me that there must have been a misapprehension at that time. At all events, doubts have since risen in the minds of some of those using the patents, and possibly operating under them, as to which is the real authority, the general act or the special act. This puts it beyond all doubt.

Radio service, to provide for the general improvement of reception conditions to licensed broadcast listeners, $180,400.
I should like to ask if it is the intention of the department to spend the total sum received for radio licences upon radio improvement or radio work in the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is the intention of the government to give the best service possible to the people of Canada. If there is a surplus it will go to the exchequer for the benefit of our country.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I was not in the chamber when the minister was explaining the radio system. Several
complaints have been received because radio owners did not know they were required to secure licences. In the rural districts some of the people have bought separate parts and put them together in an effort to build a small set, so that they may be able to entertain their friends in the evenings. Particularly in the rural districts, where storage batteries have to be recharged and the cost of radio upkeep is therefore greater, the licence fee is a burden. It may be that an inspector may come along, and seeing an aerial outside a house he will go in and ask the occupant if he has a licence. That person may reply, "No, I let my licence expire," or his answer may be that his set is not then in use.
I do not know that I have any very helpful suggestions, or that I am in a position to assist the minister, but in my humble opinion licensing of radios should be treated similarly to the licensing of motor cars. A man wdio can afford to operate a high price motor car has to pay a high rate of licence. Plenty of people on the back concessions are not financially able to buy good radios. There was a time when those people could afford to go and see a ball game or indulge in other luxurious pastimes, but to-day they have to stay at home and listen to their radios. Undoubtedly the radio offers a great deal of amusement to many people. True, they may be using a radio set somebody else has discarded; they have gathered the pieces together and put it into service. Undoubtedly the man with the cheap set should be taxed, but not as much as the man with the set costing $400 or $500. While radio listeners in the cities find that static interferes with reception, the people in the country have no difficulties of that nature. Some people own radios which bring in the programs from the most distant stations, while others can afford only those machines which have been discarded by the wealthier people and are capable of picking up only the nearby stations.
In western Ontario most of the programs come from Detroit. Programs from Detroit stations come in clearly at times when radio listeners can hear neither London nor Toronto. They never hear Ottawa. I suggest that the licence fee on high priced radios should be three dollars, and that the poorer people who have not money to buy licences should not have to pay as much. To my mind radios are in a position similar to cars in this respect.
I have seen radios that did not cost any more than $7 or $8, and it would be unfortunate if a two dollar licence Were charged on such machines. There is some justice in

the contention that if a man can afford to buy a good radio he should pay a higher licence fee. We know that the inspectors go round and visit the homes, showing their authority, and sometimes they frighten the ladies at the homes they visit. Whether the radio is used or not, however, the owner has to pay the fee.
