speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not the record here and therefore I cannot answer the question. We have so many lightkeepers that it is impossible for the minister to remember the case of each one, but if my hon. friend wants the information I can supply it on Monday.

I do not want it for myself but for my colleague from Kamouraska, who is unavoidably absent. If the minister cannot give the information now, I would ask that the vote be allowed to stand until the hon. gentleman who is interested in it has an opportunity to discuss the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I do not know that it would be fair to allow the item to stand until the hon. gentleman can be given the information. I can place the record of this man in the hands of his colleague at any time. I can say, however, that if this particular lightkeeper, Mr. Morin, has been dismissed, his dismissal must have come after a thorough investigation, and on the report of the investigator. At any rate, I shall have the record placed at the disposal of the hon. gentleman.

I regret very much that the record is not available now that the vote is
before the committee. It does not seem reasonable for the minister to ask that the item be passed without giving this information. I am well acquainted with this man Morin. I met him this summer and he assured me that he has taken no part in any election in a good many years. He was lightkeeper on one of the three Pilgrims' islands, where he was doing his duty conscientiously. He was very hospitable to all who went there either for fishing or for hunting. Indeed, he was quite friendly to all and he had friends in both parties. As a matter of fact, he did not bother at all with politics. He is a young man, very intelligent and capable, and had been appointed by the Civil Service Commission. Moreover, before the house rose at six o'clock the hon. member for Quebec East informed me that he had known the man's father, who had taken no part in politics. The minister is aware, I know, that the man was recommended by leading Conservative lawyers in Montreal whom it is unnecessary to name but who are influential with the department by reason of personal friendship and associations. All that has been ignored; why? Because of the hatred displayed by some Tories in Kamouraska county. That job was taken from Morin and given to a man who is well off, and who, I may say, is the most disagreeable man in his parish.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Who is he?
The minister knows him. Seeing that I have said something disagreeable about him, I do not wish to mention his name, but the minister knows to whom I am referring.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I should know by the record.

The minister cannot very well ask me for information when he has not given me any; I am not his deputy. Here we are voting this item blindly, and it does not' seem reasonable. Usually when a minister brings items before the committee, and particularly a minister of the hon. gentleman's standing, he has full information with him; if not, his deputy should be able to supply it. I do not wish to hlame anyone, but this is my eighth session in the house and it is the first time I have seen a minister unable to answer a pertinent question when he was piloting his estimates through the committee. I can understand that if, on the orders of the day, I ask a question of the minister in connection with the dismissal of a Mr. Morin on Pilgrims' island, he might very well reply: I will let the hon. gentleman know to-morrow or in two or three days. But the minister has had twelve months in which to prepare his estimates, and when he tells me that he will
Supply-Marine

give me the information after the item is passed, I do not think he is treating me fairly. I would direct his attention to the example set by his colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart). When that hon. gentleman is dealing with his estimates and is asked a question, he gives a full answer and not a fool answer-there is all the difference in the world. The Minister of Public Works can be cited as a minister who will always deal fairly with his colleagues in the house.
The Minister of Marine does not come from Hudson bay or the Northwest Territories, he comes from the great city of Montreal. He' occupies the honoured position of president of the Quebec Bar Association, of which I am a member. A man of his learning should know that when,' he is presenting estimates to the committee he should be prepared to supply all information required. I am very sorry, but I must puit the blame upon the minister and not upon his staff.
The general impression in the district in which I live is that this man Morin has been dealt with unfairly. This opinion is held not only iby Liberals but by good Conservatives who have never voted for me; it is thought that Morin has been dismissed for no good reason, yet when, in a polite and courteous way, I ask the minister for information in this connection, he tells me he will be ready to give it after the vote is passed. The minister may say 'that the hon. member for Kaimouraska is not here. That is quite right; he is unavoidably absent, but I am asking this question on his behalf. I may not know all the minor details of the case, 'but I am fairly well posted thereon and I know that Morin has suffered an injustice. He has been replaced by another who is not worth what 'he is receiving. I ask a question of the hon. minister and he replies by answering another question which I have asked. Apparently he wants me to give him the details of what has happened in his own department; he wants me to tell uffiat has happened in the dismissal of one man and the appointment of another. If I appointed a man, I would remember the details of his appointment.
This is a free country, and if the hon. gentleman does not give me the information I require I cannot do anything about it; but if the information is not forthcoming I cannot vote for the item. I have too much respect for the hon. gentleman to lecture him, but I am surprised at his declining to supply the information to which I am entitled and which has been asked for in the proper way, on the proper day and of the proper minister. I understand a return has been tabled in con-
[Mr. Pouliot.l
nection with this matter, and if that is so, it should be very easy for the hon. gentleman to obtain the information. I will let him in on one of the secrets of parliamentary procedure-if a return has been tabled, he can obtain a copy. If the file happens to be in the Hunter building he can obtain a copy from Mr. Horton, chief of parliamentary papers. A page could be sent to obtain the file. I do not know if this is the procedure in the Quebec assembly, but that is what is done here. I believe the hon. gentleman knows this, but he does not want us to know that he knows it. I asked the minister why this man had been dismissed, and whether such action had been taken after investigation, and he replied that if he was dismissed after an investigation it was not without good reason. I have no desire to be disagreeable or to take up too much of the time of the committee; when we ask for information, it is not to cause delay or trouble, it is only to be able to answer the questions asked of us by our constituents.

The hon. member for Temis-couata (Mr. Pouliot) is quite within his rights in asking for information with regard to dismissals by the Department of Marine. However, I take a different view from that of my hon. friend; as far as I am (personally concerned, I have not the slightest objection to a .member of the government in power or a defeated candidate recommending to a minister that a certain official be dismissed. The only objection I do raise in this regard is that this or any other government should be hypocritical about the matter. The Prime Minister believes in economy and is practising it to a -certain extent, but I am -going to ask him to go a little further in his practice. During the past year tens of thousands of dollars have been wasted -by the different departments in investigating the actions of public servants. As I said a moment ago, I have no objection if a defeated candidate or a member supporting -the government recommends to any minister that , the occupan-cy of a certain office be changed; I sit back and take my medicine, and . tell my friends that that is ail that they are entitled to. But I do object to any minister or any government spending thousands of dollars for no good purpose. In the province of Nova Scotia, for instance, a number of lightkeepers, postmasters and others have been dismissed, -and it is nothing short of scandalous the amount of money paid these investigators who go round and hold investigations with their minds made up before-

Supply-M arine
hand as to what they are going to do-they know they are going to recommend dismissal. I say to the minister, to the Prime Minister and the government that they should stop that practice, and let the minister concerned take the responsibility and dismiss any Grit he wants to.
This vote is for the construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation, including salaries and allowances of light-keeipers. I note that there is a decrease in this vote from last year of $494,600, and I would like the minister after I sit down to be good enough to explain to the committee how that reduction is made up. He will notice that the first part of the item refers to the construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation. Now, if there is one important service in this country it is that which has to. do with aids to navigation, whether they are on the Atlantic coast, the Great lakes, in the river St. Lawrence or on the Pacific. I trust the minister will be able to tell the committee that in spite of this reduction no instructions will be issued to those in charge of our marine agencies that aids to navigation are not to be put where they are necessary, because the whole marine life of this country depends upon aids to navigation along our coasts and in our navigable waters.
The second part of the item refers to the salaries and allowances of lightkeepers. I assume that part of the reduction is made up of the general ten per cent cut in salaries. I would plead with the minister, with the Prime Minister and with the Minister of Finance, in view of the fact that the Minister of Finance was good enough on Wednesday last to move that the committee rise and report progress on the bill reducing civil servants' salaries, that before we proceed any further with that bill it be determined that no reduction be made in the salaries of lightkeepers. Do the minister, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance realize what these lightkeepers all along our coasts and in the river St. Lawrence have to put up with? Take my hon. friend from Cape Breton North-Victoria, in whose constituency I believe St. Paul's island is. The lightkeepers are out there in the gulf of the St. Lawrence, one hundred miles from civilization, with no chance for their children to go to school, isolated practically the whole year; yet the minister and the government are going to cut their salaries by ten per cent. Take the lightkeepers on Sable island, the worst place in God's world for any person to live; and yet the lightkeepers who are there from one year's end to another, sometimes 41761-117
coming back fit for no other occupation, are to lose ten per cent of their salaries. It is a shame and disgrace, Mr Chairman, that any government or parliament should dare to cut the salaries of these men. The same thing applies to every lightkeeper in the country. Some of them are doing this work for only two hundred dollars a year, and you are going to cut their salaries ten per cent. Some of the ilightkeepers who were receiving salaries of $800 had their salaries cut last year to $420, and now the government proposes to cut them still further by ten per cent. I say it is not right. Surely the Prime Minister and the Finance minister, if they want to economize, can save in some other direction rather than that of taking the bread out of the mouths of the lightkeepers on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, in the gulf of the St. Lawrence and the Great lakes. I plead with the Prime Minister, the Finance minister and the Minister of Marine to allow this item to stand, or that the Minister of Marine bring down an item in the supplementary estimates so that the salaries of these lightkeepers shall nob be reduced by one cent.

I have, much pleasure in
supporting the suggestion made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough. Certainly the life saving service is the last place where we should try to economize. We might perhaps with the consent of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough substitute the lightkeepers for the lieutenant-governors in the civil service salary reduction bill exempting the lightkeepers from the cut and bringing the lieutenant-governors under it. I think the general public of Canada would appreciate that.
I would like to make a very mild protest at the remarks of my hon. friend from Temis-couata. If I understood him aright, he had the idea that the intelligence, of Canada was centralized in Montreal and that the further you went from that city the less gray matter was possessed by hon. members. I would ask the minister if he has taken any steps to carry out the promise which he was kind enough to give us last year. He will find the matter to which I refer recorded in Hansard of May 21 last. I notice that I was supported on that occasion by the hon. member for Pariy Sound, who spoke

Supply-M arine

very strongly on the matter. Put briefly, the situation is this. The lighthouse keepers are. of course, civil servants, and there is an arrangement between this government and the provincial governments that if the lighthouse keeper meets with death or accident in his duties the Dominion government will pay to the workmen's compensation board of the province concerned, such a sum as, capitalized, will enable the workmen's compensation board of that province to pay the proper pension or compensation just as if the man had been employed in ordinary industrial work. But a case arises in which that is not possible, and that is the case of the lighthouse keepers' assistants. They are not paid by the Dominion government except indirectly, although really they may be considered as being paid by the federal authorities. The way it is done is this: the lighthouse keeper is paid a salary which is, supposedly, sufficiently large to enable him to employ one or more assistants. But the extra allowance for the assistant is so small that the ordinary lighthouse keeper cannot find an able-bodied man to do the work at the price, consequently he has to fall back on some member of his family, a growing boy or his wife-because the work is generally not very hard-or some old man he happens to know. The lighthouse keeper pays to such assistant a small sum, and it has been ruled that because of that, the assistant is not in the employ of the federal authorities. I brought the question up last year and represented that it was rather a hardship on these lighthouse keepers' assistants, who were subject to the same risks as the lighthouse keepers themselves, that if they were killed or injured in their occupation there would be no compensation or pension paid, and the suggestion was made by myself and the hon. member for Parry Sound that the government should pay the lighthouse keeper a few extra dollars-it would only be a few extra dollars a year, not a month-to enable the lighthouse keeper to pay to the workmen's compensation board the fee current in that province. It is always optional for them to do that even in occupations where the workmen's compensation legislation does not ordinarily apply. I am glad to say that the matter was fully discussed and that the minister spoke as follows:
The question is very important and I will give consideration to it.
I should be glad to know if the minister has taken it into consideration, and if so, with what results.

Answering my hon.

I wonder if the

I desire, Mr. Chairman,
to express to the minister my appreciation of his attitude to-night. I desire to commend especially to his kind attention the case of

Mr. MaeINNIS: Before this item carries I should like to say a few words in connection with a matter which I think comes under it. I refer to the inspection of tackle used in loading and unloading ships.
The minister will remember that earlier in the session I placed a question on the order paper with regard to the intention of the minister as to the bringing down of legislation in this connection. The question was whether the minister had received from the Vancouver harbour commission a draft copy of safety regulations applicable to the loading and unloading of ships, together with the recommendation that these be made a by-law of the harbour board. The minister informed me that this communication had been received but that the by-law could not be approved by the department because they had obtained an opinion from the Department of Justice holding that the Vancouver harbour commissioners were not competent to draw up such a by-law.
In this connection, Mr. Chairman, may I say that a large number of people are engaged in what we call longshore work, the loading and Unloading of ships, and although their work is extremely hazardous, as I will show by statistics furnished by the compensation board of British Columbia, there are no safety regulations covering that work. The municipalities in which this work is carried on claim that they have no jurisdiction in
the matter of making regulations; the provincial government says it has no jurisdiction, and now the Department of Justice maintains that the harbour commisisoners have no jurisdiction either. So we find that these men are working under conditions which are extremely dangerous, and there is no one who can enforce safety regulations.
Some time ago a conciliation board was considering an agreement between the waterfront workers of the city of Vancouver and the stevedoring association. One of the present members of the Vancouver harbour commisison, Mr. Thompson, was a member of that conciliation board, and that board recommended that such safety regulations should be made. I should like to read from a statement submitted to that board by the chairman of the workmen's compensation board of British Columbia in response to a request for information. This letter is dated June 18, 1930, and is addressed to Mr. J. B. Thompson, chairman of the conciliation board which was sitting at that time. Mr. Winn, chairman of the Compensation board of British Columbia writes:
Referring to your telephone conversation today, we find on looking up our records that as far back as 1919, we endeavoured to obtain the appointment of a tackle inspector for this port. In recent years we have also taken up such an appointment with the Vancouver harbour commissioners.
The board is without jurisdiction to deal with such matters as come under the heading of navigation and shipping, that being distinctly a matter over which the federal government, either through its various departments or through the harbour commission, has sole authority.
It is, we believe, self apparent that an independent inspector having to do with the inspection of tackle, equipment and proper lighting and having authority to enforce regulations, is the one who should deal with all accident prevention matters.
The chief efficacy of such an inspector is that he would be an independent arbiter as to the means to -be used to safeguard the life and limbs of workmen. One cannot get the same independence of thought and action from an employee that die would expect from an independent official. We have undertaken to supervise,-
That is, the compensation board have undertaken to supervise.
-without cost to the department or commission making the appointment, the work of such an inspector so as to ensure uniformity of direction as well as fair treatment to all. We have on our commission and staff competent engineers who, by reason of their accident prevention experience, would be able to hold a firm hand on any official so appointed, and in this way ensure competency. Inasmuch as our board is the one to collect funds and to pay for disabilities we are naturally more able to keep close supervision over those matters which go to accident prevention.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I should like the minister to pay particular attention to this paragraph:
As it is now, a foreign boat may come into the harbour with defective tackle and equipment; may employ its own longshoremen, kill or maim them and then leave (unless it is libelled by the injured workman or his representative), without in any way accounting for its casualties, thus leaving the cost to be borne by our citizens. The average longshoreman in case of serious disability-and I take it we would be in much the same position-does _ not think of his legal rights until he feels the pinch of need. By that time the ship has gone.
I should like to point out that in a case of that kind the injured person or his dependents would be entitled to no compensation whatever. On the other hand, of course, if a longshoreman were employed by one of the stevedoring companies having its head office in some part of British Columbia, he would be entitled to compensation. Mr. Winn points that out; he says:
On the other hand, if the boat in question employs one of our stevedoring companies then the stevedoring company and its employees are covered by the Workmen's Compensation Act, and the result is that in event of accident the workman is compensated.
Now I wish to give some figures with regard to accidents, and also to give illustrations of the causes that lead lip to accidents. I have the figures from 1918 to 1930, but I will not take the time of the house reading them all. If it were possible, I should like to put them on Hansard without reading them, but if I am not allowed to do so I will content myself with quoting them in part.
In 1918, the first year on record, there were 239 claims. Of these there were seven permanent or partial disability awards and one fatal accident. The total cost in that year was 817,666. By 1923 the number of accidents had increased to 388, with twelve permanent or partial disability awards; there were no fatal accidents in that year. The total cost was over $36,000. I would observe here that up to 1923-I cannot speak for any point outside Vancouver-'the longshoremen of that city were strongly organized, and in the fail or early winter of that year there was a strike in longshore work. The workers' organizations were defeated. Now I want .to show what difference that made in the number of accidents that occurred in the following year when the men were without an organization to protect .the worker. As I have pointed out, the total claims in 1923 were 388, with twelve permanent or partial disability awards; and there were no fatal accidents in that year. The total cost, as I have stated, was over $36,000. Now, in 1924 the number of claims totalled 536, with twelve permanent or partial dis-
(Mr. Maclnnis.]
ability awards and ten fatal accidents, and the total cost was over $119,000.
Generally speaking, from 1924 up to the present time accidents have been increasing, along with the cost; so that in 1930, the last year for which I have figures, there were 582 claims, with forty permanent or partial disability awards and three fatal accidents, involving a total cost of $152,000. It seems to me, in face of such a condition, that the minister should take steps to have the lives and limbs of men engaged in this sort of work protected.
The chairman of the compensation board of British Columbia stated that the only competent authority in (the matter was the federal government, through some of its departments, and undoubtedly the Department of Marine is the one under which this should come. I hold that under section 674 of the Canada Shipping Act the minister has power even now to make regulations in that regard if he thinks fit. I shall read that section, and if it does not fully cover the situation, them I .think that minor amendments could be made to render it applicable. It .could easily foe amended to serve the purpose intended. The section reads:
Every inspector may, at any time, visit any ship, whether registered in Canada or elsewhere, and whether propelled wholly or in part by steam, except ships belonging to His Majesty; and although any such ship is classed in Lloyds register of British and foreign shipping, or in any other corporation or association for the survey and register of ships approved by the governor in council, may inspect and examine the tackle, machinery or apparatus used for the loading or unloading thereof, and, if he considers such tackle, machinery or apparatus defective, so as to be dangerous to life, he shall report thereon to the minister, who may order that such tackle, machinery and apparatus shall not be used until permitted by the minister.
I suppose when the act says "may report" to the minister, that means either to the minister or to his representative in the locality; for it would be a very slow process if a report had to come from Vancouver or from Halifax to the department here in order that instructions might be sent as to what should be done. As regards the words "may inspect and examine", I should think that the minister might very well construe that as "shall", and that would serve the purpose.
Under that section of the Canada Shipping Act, the minister has jurisdiction and the necessary means to fulfil the requirements for safety. I believe that the Vancouver harbour commissioners are favourable to safety regulations. I understand that in November, 1931, they forwarded a copy of rather full regulations for the approval of the minister. They

Sup-ply-Marine
wanted to have these regulations approved as a by-law. I believe that, while the harbour commissioners have not the power to draft and enforce regulations, if these by-laws were approved by the minister they would have the effect of departmental regulations and could be made applicable under the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. I am not a lawyer but I take it that this could be done, once the regulations had the approval of the minister. There are twenty-five sections in these regulations, which were approved by the Vancouver harbour commissioners, by the workmen's compensation board, by the council of thei city of Vancouver and by the waterfront workers themselves, through their association; so that they are opposed only by the stevedore companies of the province of British Columbia. The last section of the resolutions of the Vancouver harbour commission reads as follows:
The safety inspector shall have authority to inspect all loading and unloading berths and the equipment thereon, and shall have authority to prohibit work if he considers conditions unsafe.
I think that is a perfectly reasonable authority to give, and it should be given in this instance. In most other industries in the province of British Columbia the workmen's compensation board has authority and can enforce safety regulations. I have in my hand a copy of a letter addressed to the Minister of Marine by the assistant secretary of the workmen's compensation board of [DOT] the province of British Columbia, and which deals with the matter I am now discussing. It is rather lengthy, but it gives a very good picture of the conditions which prevail. The minister may have forgotten having received this letter, and I bring it to his attention,. It is dated November 14, 1931, and reads:
On or about the 23rd ultimo, we were informed that the Shipping Federation of British Columbia which, we understand is composed of employers engaged in stevedoring in or about Vancouver, wrote you opposing the appointment of an accident prevention inspector for this port.
Experience throughout the continent has emphasized the supreme importance of accident prevention as the surest and soundest way of curtailing human wastage in industry and to reduce for the employers the cost of accidents in lengthy time loss, medical attention, increased labour turnover, permanent disabilities and loss of life. Each accident prevented and each safeguard installed means not only a reduction of the strain on the funds of the industry hut also the saving and preserving of manpower both to the province and to the nation. An accident prevention inspector would be continually carrying on an educational safety campaign, which could not help but develop a "safety consciousness" and therefore a more careful and efficient employee.
At times in the past we know that the Vancouver Harbour Commission has had a safety inspector, but his only authority, as we gather from him, has been to report to them any unsafe practices or unsafe equipment. He would also advise officials in charge of the work as to dangerous places and practices, but he had no authority whatsoever to insist upon any remedies.
The Vancouver harbour commission is trying to do whatever it possibly can in this connection, and, as is pointed out by this letter, it has appointed at its own cost a man to inspect the equipment used in the loading and unloading of ships. But this inspector has no authority to enforce any regulations after he has found a defect in the equipment used; all he can do is direct attention to such defect and try to prevail upon the shipping federation to discontinue the use of such defective equipment. The letter continues :
We know too that the shipping federation has had a safety inspector. In discussing the matter with him we were informed that his only authority was to advise his employers of the various hazards undergone from time to time by the workmen and to, at times, recommend an alleviation. He had no power of a definite nature to cause the remedy of any dangerous or faulty equipment, nor to insist upon the prevention of unsafe practices. It is apparent that he occupied an unenviable position, because from time to time he would be in the position of having to advise his employers that their equipment was faulty or that the vessels employing these firms to do their work had dangerous machinery or poor equipment. In advising his employers of defective equipment he would be, in effect, asking them to expend money to remedy such conditions. The possibilities were that his employers would not care to insist upon those in charge of the incoming vessels stopping work to repair or replace faulty machinery or equipment. If the inspector were active in accident prevention measures, it can be quite easily understood that he could not hope to hold his position for any length of time.
The holding of a position is an important matter in these hard times, and this so-called inspector would not be very keen to detect defective equipment. The letter continues:
From the foregoing it is apparent that a great part of the work of either of the above inspectors would be abortive by reason of his lack of authority.
The Workmen's Compensation Act of British Columbia has been in effect approximately fifteen shears. When it had been in effect for about two years it 'became apparent from evidence taken in hearings on accident cases, from complaints received from workmen, from reports of accidents on our records, that there was a very great need for definite accident

speechtext:
prevention measures in stevedoring work. In 1919 we started to take steps to bring to the attention of your department, through representatives, the necessity for greater protection on the Vancouver waterfront.
Although the minister has not been in office since 1919, I would direct his attention to the fact that since that year the workmen's compensation board has been drawing this matter to the attention of the federal Department of Marine, yet nothing has been done and the workers are being killed and maimed in accidents, many of which could be prevented. The letter continues:
Frequently since that time, as the opportunity presented itself we have joined with other interested parties in seeking to achieve the same end. We believe that as a result of these efforts the hereinbefore mentioned inspectors were appointed, but with their lack of jurisdiction of a mandatory nature it^ was realized that their efforts were mainly fruitless. It is true, however, that some faulty gear and some unsafe practices were remedied.
The Vancouver and District Waterfront Workers' Association, as our records indicate, endeavoured on a number of occasions to obtain the sought for objective, the federal appointment of accident prevention inspectors. They were joined in their efforts by the Amalgamated Carpenters of Canada;-
These carpenters are employed in lining ships to be used for the shipment of grain, and have to work under the same hazardous conditions as the longshoremen. The letter continues:
-the Canadian Merchant Service Guild, composed of captains, masters, mates, etc., operating in our coastal waters; the British Columbia Safety League, whose sole objective is the prevention of accidents, and the city of Vancouver.
Everyone connected with the business carried on in the shipping district of ,the city of Vancouver is interested in the drafting and putting into effect of regulations which will prevent accidents on the waterfront. The letter continues:

I should like to impress upon the committee the seriousness of the situation which exists on the waterfront in Vancouver, though some hon. members may think the matter is of no particular importance. It is several years since I brought up this very question on the floor of the house and received assurances from the minister then in charge that something would be done. However, nothing has been done, and the situation is a serious one. It seems as if the responsibility for accident does not rest with any one party. At times it is the harbour board that is held responsible, at other times it is the Dominion government, and so on. To use the ordinary slang phrase, it is a case of passing the buck. In the meantime there are a great many accidents, and there is no safeguard for the waterfront workers. I speak rather feelingly in the matter because I know the situation very intimately. I know some of the men engaged in this work; I know how much they realize the need for protection of this kind, and I trust the committee will take seriously this letter which is being read and the representations which are being made. I hope the hon. member will now be allowed to continue.

I am quoting from this letter, Mr. Chairman, because it puts the case much better than I could put it myself. All I am interested in is in making the best possible case for the waterfront workers, in the province of British Columbia in particular, but also in other parts of the dominion. I am not talking just for the sake of filling up time. I have never done that, and I have no intention of doing it to-night. Quoting from the letter:
The board does not keep a list of accidents happening in any particular locality, but to prove the need we have, out of a mass of waterfront accidents, looked up- the files and selected a few of the cases to which some of the regulations would apply. Attached hereto and under the number of the particular section of the proposed by-laws is a list of a few cases that have actually happened in the last two years, and which could have been remedied had there been a safety inspector qualified and fully authorized to act as an independent arbitrator in seeing to it that faulty gear and equipment and unsafe practices were not used or operated.
Then it goes on to give the cost rates charged to employers engaged in stevedoring work in British Columbia from 1924 to 1931. I shall not read all the figures, but simply wish to point out that in 1924 the charge was 84.87 per $100 of pay-roll, and in 1931 it had almost doubled, amounting to $8 per $100 of pay-roll. That is sufficient, Mr. Chairman,
to show the increasing seriousness of waterfront accidents in the province of British Columbia. Quoting again from the letter:
The above figures indicate the increase in number and severity of accidents in the last five years. As you know, therefore, no profits under workmen's compensation and moneys are only collected from employers as required to meet the cost of accidents. While it is true that these rates cover all of the stevedoring operations in the province, yet examination or the record of the various employers in and about Vancouver gives no general indication that their experience is in any way different from the experience of employers operating elsewhere. Substantially two-thirds of the accidents that happen in the stevedoring industry occur in the port of Vancouver. In the case of some of the vessels where serious accidents have happened elsewhere these same vessels in completing their cargo took a portion of it a.t Vancouver, so that, for example, if a workman's leg were crushed and possibly amputated by reason of faulty gear or equipment on the vessel at some other port, the same condition could have happened on the same ship in the port of Vancouver.
During the arbitration between the Vancouver and District Waterfront Workers' Association and the Employers in the port of Vancouver in June, 1930, the whole situation was very fully discussed with Mr. J. B. Thomson, who was then chairman of the arbitration committee, and is now a member of the Vancouver harbour commission, and we are sure that he was very fully convinced of the necessity of the course outlined herein.
He was undoubtedly convinced to the extent that in 1931 he forwarded to the department for the approval of the minister the regulations I have already mentioned. Quoting again from the letter, I read the following:
Our board, through its chairman, advised Mr. Thomson under date of June 18, 1930, that it was self apparent that an independent accident prevention inspector having authority to enforce regulations should be the one to deal with the inspection of tackle, equipment, proper lighting and all accident prevention matters, together with the necessary accident prevention education which would be brought about by his frequent visits to the various docks throughout this district. It was then pointed out that the chief efficacy of such an inspector was that he would be an independent arbiter as to the means to be used to safeguard life and limbs of workmen. It is quite apparent we believe that one cannot get the same independence of thought and action from an employee that one would expect from an independent official. The board's viewpoint has been concurred in, as outlined before, by all parties having to do with the actual work on the -waterfront, save the employers in question.
Might we suggest that the passing of the proposed harbour board regulations could not act detrimentally to the port of Vancouver. We fail to find a single regulation that can be said to be extreme or arbitrary or that would place any additional penalty on a vessel coming into this harbour other than is necessary

Is there any doubt but that in the average case of disability -and I take it we would be in the same position-a workman does not think of his rights until he feels the pinch of need, by which time the vessel might be gone from our shores.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has occupied an hour's time in reading communications which are on the files of the department, and in connection with which those of us who are in close touch with this matter have full and complete knowledge. For the past few months the minister in charge, myself and others who 
have taken a direct interest in this matter -.more than merely talking about it on one or two occasions-have been endeavouring to find a suitable way of dealing with this matter, for which we have been desirous of seeking a remedy. At first it was thought that the by-law of the harbour commissioners to which the hon. member has referred on so many occasions to-night might have been the proper way to deal with it. However, after the by-law had been formulated, forwarded to Ottawa, and examined by officers of the department, it was learned that the harbour commissioners did not have the jurisdiction which we had at first supposed. Under such by-law it would have been useless to appoint inspectors, 'because the first case challenged would of course have disclosed the weakness of the whole procedure. Then the minister, his staff and myself sought other means to deal with the situation. It was hoped that amendments to the Canada Shipping Act might have been prepared for this session. That procedure was delayed, however, as hon. members know, because of the very extensive nature of the changes due to the statute of Westminster, which was completed only a .few months ago. During the past week or two the minister and his officials have been studying the matter, and only yesterday I was in touch with the Department of Marine in connection with it. Possibly the situation may be met in part by instructing the inspectors of ship hulls and boilers to enlarge their inspections so as to include tackle. Personally I think there is still some question as to the soundness of that procedure-I will not say the advisability of it, but as to whether or not authority goes that far. It is thought, however, that the difficulty may be met in that way until such time as the general shipping act is amended, or until power could be given to the harbour board to pass regulations.
I wish to assure the committee that this matter has been under close observation and study by the department, its officials, the minister and myself, and has not in any sense been neglected. It must be recognized that in matters of this kind a pious wish that something be done is not sufficient; there is the question of working out the constitutional and technical details. True, we sometimes express a little irritation at delays, but in this instance I think the delays have been warranted, and every possible effort has been made to meet the situation. I do not know that anything further can be said on the subject at the present time. The minister, I know, will support me in what I say, that

Supply-Marine
without any unreasonable delay the matter will be completed. I might also add that there have been some changes in the senior officials of the Marine department which has made correspondence and discussions a bit awkward, because Mr. Johnston retired a little while ago, the deputy was ill for some time and the present acting deputy comes on the job without having knowledge of what has passed between myself and the other officials. This has caused delay, regrettable no doubt, but nothing further, I think, could have been done under the circumstances.
I regret the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to go out of his way to find fault with the time I had occupied in bringing the matter to his attention, but I did not take even thirty minutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: A solid hour.

There were less than five pages in the letter, and I did not read the whole of it. I am not a very fast reader but 1 can read more than five pages in an hour. I pointed out that this matter had been before the department since 1919, that the present Minister of Marine had not been in office during part of that time, and that I was not finding any great fault with him, but simply drawing it to his attention. Surely we have the right to draw to the attention of the committee matters which affect the life and limb of workers in their daily avocations without being accused of taking up too much time.

I heartily support the very able presentation of this case made by the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis). I do not quite grasp what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said as to what action would be taken. He said they contemplated giving authority to the steamboat and hull inspectors by enlarging their jurisdiction to include the inspection of tackle, but I understood him to say there was some possible objection even to that. If that is the case, the obvious remedy would be to amend the Canada Shipping Act in its entirety this session. But while that might not ibe possible, it would be quite simple to pass what I might term an interim revision of such sections of the act as deal with this matter. Do not let us have any mistake so that after parliament has adjourned we shall find that for another year the government is prevented from taking the necessary action. It would be a very simple matter to pass an amendment. Indeed I understood the minister to say on another occasion he was going to amend the Canada Shipping Act this session dealing with some specific thing which he named. If that is so, it would be very easy
for him to take authority to do what is required to give full force and weight to whatever action may be necessary regarding this matter. I agree entirely with the member for Vancouver South, that it is of no use to appoint a man merely to advise these people. Some of these tramp steamer people are not open to advice; they will simply laugh at him. The hon. member read some regulations, one of which said the inspector should report any case to the minister, and he assumed that that would not mean reporting to the minister at Ottawa. To my mind it would, and it would foe highly undesirable to have the thing hung uip while the report was going to Ottawa, because in that time the boat would be loaded, somebody might be killed, and the boat would have sailed. Surely we should give the inspector power to order an immediate change in the tackle or other equipment, if faulty, and then if his action is found to be too arbitrary it would be subject to revision later on. That would ensure safety for the men in the meantime. I am much interested in this matter because we have the same situation on the west coast, where we are loading a large number of ships every year. Port Alberni is now the third largest shipping port in British Columbia, which gives an idea of the amount of business done there. We aTe having too mimy accidents. But you cannot^ expect one ship to go to considerable expense if others are not compelled to do so. Put them all on an even basis and give the inspector ample powers.
The member for Vancouver South, spoke of the workmen's compensation board having a safety officer. I had an opportunity on one occasion to observe the action of such an officer. I was coming down from a logging camp some years ago, and even to my untrained eye the roadbed was in a horrible condition. I said to the lad who was on the speeder bringing me down, "This roadbed is in a rotten condition." He said, "Yes, that is what the safety inspector told the boss yesterday." I made inquiries and found that the inspector had condemned a mile and a half of that track, and he did not allow an engine to move over it until the track was put in a proper state. Probably that saved a bad accident. There is no kick among the lumber people, for those who are alive to their responsibilities realize it is a good thing, and in the long run, economical, to have a man in that capacity. He does not ask unreasonable things, but he is down on the men who, as they say in lumber circles, run a "haywire" proposition. That is the sort of power we want to give the inspector in connection with the stevedore operations.

If the eastern ports desire to obtain a greater volume of Canadian grain they must instil the same confidence in those who will use their ports as is now felt in those terminals which are under the control of the grain board. Has the minister any information as to whether or not the harbour commissions at Montreal, St. John or Halifax have registered any objection to coming completely under the jurisdiction of the Board of Grain Commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The ports of Halifax, St. John and Montreal are as completely under the jurisdiction of the Board of Grain Commissioners as is possible under the grain act as at present drafted. The mistake, if I may call it such, in the reasoning of my hon. friend is this: Vancouver, Prince Rupert and Port Arthur are what are known as inspection points at which inspection certificates are issued'-terminal inspection certificates are not issued at the eastern outlets, as this would already be done at Port Arthur or Fort William. There is a question as to the advisability of making these eastern ports inspection points, and to do so would require an amendment to the act.
Do I. understand that as far as outward cargoes are concerned, there is no inspection at any of these three ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.
The certificate is merely transferred from Port Arthur or some other inspection point?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The certificate follows the grain.
What has been the experience with regard to complaints in connection with outward cargoes shipped from these ports, as compared with shipments from Vancouver or Prince Rupert?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For some years the conditions have been very satisfactory.

Considerable discussion has
taken place in the newspapers as to why more grain should not pass through the port of Halifax. It would be very informative if the minister could state to the committee the policy of the government in regard to endeavouring to have more grain shipped through that port.
